chunks: that Amir Al-Momineen (peace be upon him) used to judge regarding an atheist (Zindiq) when two just, acceptable witnesses testify against him, and a thousand testify for him with his freedom/exemption; he accepted the testimony of the two men and invalidated the testimony of the thousand because it is an undisclosed religion.

key_terms.الزِّنْدِيقِ: Atheist or heretic (specifically one who hides their disbelief)

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia legal ruling on the testimony of two versus a thousand witnesses in the case of an atheist?
ai.summary: This ruling by Imam Ali (AS) in *Al-Kafi* highlights the jurisprudential principle that for 'hidden' religions (*din makum*), such as atheism or Zoroastrianism, the standard of proof relies on the credibility of a few just witnesses rather than the quantity of witnesses, as widespread public knowledge is unlikely. This contrasts with cases like Islam, where testimony is often based on public declaration, underscoring the Shia scholarly distinction between *Zindiq* (often implying hidden apostasy or dualism) and the general apostate. The hadith illustrates the practical application of *shahada* (testimony) in early Islamic courts to determine religious status when internal belief is not immediately visible.

en.hubeali: ‘Amir Al-Momineen<sup>asws</sup> had judged regarding an atheist when two just, acceptable witnesses testify against him, they testify for him a thousand with the freeing him. He<sup>asws</sup> allowed the testimony of two men and invalidated the testimonies of a thousand because it is an undisclosed religion’.
